Welcome to State of the Day,

Wall Street’s favorite monsters have some very powerful friends in the Beltway

Washington Is Talking Tough. Wall Street Has Heard This Before.

Private equity, the industry built around buying businesses, restructuring them, and selling them for a profit, has got lawmakers on the Hill antsy again.

But don’t get your hopes up.

These firms — the closest thing to real-life monsters on Wall Street — have massive impacts on the businesses they swallow up. For decades, critics have argued firms are more interested in squeezing every last dollar out of a company, leaving things like long-term viability, customer satisfaction, and cultural significance on the back burner.

Now, a few starry-eyed lawmakers want to put the brakes on the profit machine.

Congress did pass a bipartisan housing law this year that restricts these types of firms from buying up single-family homes. But hidden in the fine print is a parting gift: institutional investors get to keep the homes they’ve already bought.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren also reintroduced her Stop Wall Street Looting Act, which would make private equity firms responsible for certain debts and liabilities of the businesses they take over. She’s even teamed up with Republican Sen. Josh Hawley on a separate bill targeting consolidation in health care.

But hold your horses. Before you get excited that Washington might actually be fixing a problem for once, let’s look at their track record with these guys.

The Wall Street monsters wield a big stick in the Beltway, and their friends have helped the industry keep their sticky fingers on some of their most lucrative loopholes.

When legislators on the Hill even think about touching private equity’s money, an army of lobbyists bankrolled by these firms comes running and suddenly the proposed reforms vanish.

Take carried interest, a tax break that lets private-equity fund managers pay the lower capital-gains tax rate on certain investment profits instead of the much higher ordinary-income rate. Basically, one of those lovely little loopholes that helps the people who already have more money than they know what to do with keep even more of it.

And the fighters on Capitol Hill have been endlessly debating how to close this loophole for decades.

What do they have to show for it? Nada.

In 2007, the industry’s biggest firms and their trade association hired 20 lobbying firms to fight proposed carried-interest reforms. Blackstone alone spent $4.9 million on lobbying that year, according to a ProPublica investigation.

And it worked: the measure died in the Senate; legislators tried again in 2010, only to fail again.

And neither party’s hands are clean here. Just a few years ago, in 2022, then-Senator Kyrsten Sinema hedged her support for President Biden’s Inflation Reduction Act on the contingency that a provision which would have narrowed the aforementioned carried interest tax breaks be dropped.

Her party obliged and nixed the provision. The Wall Street monsters rejoiced.

President Trump actually campaigned on ending the loophole when he first ran for president.

At the time, Trump called the loophole “so good for Wall Street investors, and for people like me, but unfair to American workers.” But his 2017 tax cuts left the enriching mechanism largely intact, and once again the Wall Street monsters celebrated.

Another day, another Washington promise that didn’t quite pan out. And another loss for the people who can’t afford to hire an army of lobbyists to protect their bottom line.

So it’s fair to take a skeptical look at any new attempts to rein in these wealth monsters. It’s easy for politicians to talk tough, but what do they actually accomplish?

Some have characterized the upcoming midterms as a wake-up call for private equity, with everyone in the Beltway besides Speaker Johnson expecting a night full of Democratic wins. The idea that a referendum on private equity is near has grown in popularity.

But history tells us a different story, as does the nature of the swamp.

You ask me? This wave of tough talk might give us a few spineless bills here and there. The loopholes private equity treasures the most? I’m not holding my breath.

Washington runs on money, and private equity has spent decades playing enough inside baseball to make sure they’ve always got a seat at the table.

So a few lawmakers want to take on the Wall Street monsters, make them sweat for a change?

Let’s see if they have the stomach to follow through.

Trump’s Triumphs — Steve Sailer, SteveSailer.Net

Steve Sailer noticed something curious about the New York Times editorial board’s latest 2,000-word screed against President Trump: the things it didn’t complain about. The same paper that spent 2020 obsessing over systemic racism, police brutality, affirmative action and transgender rights somehow managed to avoid all those subjects in its latest anti-Trump manifesto. Sailer argues the omissions say as much about Trump’s policy successes — and the left’s changing priorities — as the criticisms themselves.

Dem Mayor Revives Pre-2008 Mortgage Playbook That Helped Fuel Housing Crisis — Jack McGeever, Daily Caller News Foundation

Giving hundreds of thousands of dollars to borrowers with poor credit while giving them low down payments: what could go wrong? Philadelphia Mayor Cherelle Parker announced a new publicly-backed mortgage program for residents that has eerie similarities to the lending practices that led to the 2008 financial crisis. The Daily Caller News Foundation’s Jack McGeever dives into the concerning proposal coming out of the city of brotherly love.

Inside Democrats’ Secret Effort to Stack Alaska’s Ballot — Kellen Browning, New York Times

The New York Times uncovered text messages and insider accounts implicating Democrat Mary Peltola’s campaign and national Democratic operatives in an election plot to recruit a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to run against the Republican senator of the same name. The apparent goal was to confuse voters and siphon votes away from the incumbent. Peltola’s campaign previously denied involvement. The revelations come less than a week before Election Day.

What Most Women Get Wrong About Satisfying Sex — Mary Rooke, Daily Caller

While some women call it quits on their marriages once things get … stale … the Daily Caller’s Mary Rooke makes the case for sticking around and putting in the work. Personable and witty as usual, Rooke lays out the cultural shift that has captured the modern woman’s psyche. As she so eloquently puts it, “The easiest option is to leave. But the better option is to let him touch you.”

Everyone sits in the same traffic now — Yancey Strickler, The Ideaspace

Yancey Strickler dives into what he calls the “Robert Mosesification” of the internet: the shift from collaboration to extraction. The same handful of tech giants have turned the internet’s once-sprawling neighborhoods into a few massive highways designed to keep us scrolling, shopping, and feeding their bottom lines. Now AI threatens to accelerate that trend, turning the open web into a resource for bots to harvest rather than a place for people to explore. The internet used to be a global village. Now we’re all stuck in the same traffic.

news.originalContent:
Image not from story(Photo by Jefferson Siegel-Pool/Getty Images)

A federal judge in Texas faces a misconduct investigation and a court-ordered psychiatric exam after she told a Latino civil rights attorney he was intimidated by “black excellence.”

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown repeatedly described attorney Ezra Young as white during an April 24 hearing in Dallas, according to the court transcript. Young, who is Latino, represented a black law professor in a tenure dispute with Southern Methodist University, Bloomberg Law reported.

During the April hearing, Brown said Young carried “white privilege” and showed “white mediocrity,” according to the transcript. She called him a “white savior, come to save all the stupid black lawyers in Texas who need your help, from New York.” (RELATED: Judge Strikes Down New York’s Body Armor Ban)

Young told the court he had disclosed his ethnicity more than once. “I’m not white, Your Honor,” he said.

A lawyer’s misconduct complaint against US District Judge Ada Brown stemmed from a hearing during which she repeatedly directed racial insults at him, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg Law. https://t.co/ESjtACRkIJ

Young filed a complaint against Brown soon after the hearing, according to Bloomberg Law. He wrote that the judge might have a mental health condition. The filing helped trigger an inquiry that cost Brown her docket this month.

The Fifth Circuit’s judicial council reassigned her cases Sept. 29 and blocked new assignments for three months, the Dallas Express reported. Investigators ordered a psychiatric evaluation and found she had withdrawn from more than 40 cases.

Brown then emailed sealed court records to roughly 140 judges, lawyers and reporters, according to Bloomberg Law. A special committee led by Fifth Circuit Chief Judge Jennifer Walker Elrod has ordered her to appear. The panel warned it could proceed without her cooperation.

Brown has denied wrongdoing in a 76-page response and rejected any claim of a mental health problem, according to Bloomberg Law. She said she could have handled the race discussion “more delicately.”

Andre Davis, a former federal appeals judge, said the case for removing Brown “would be compelling” if the probe closed on the current record, according to Bloomberg Law. Arthur Hellman, a judicial ethics scholar at the University of Pittsburgh, said judges should remain “patient, dignified, respectful, and courteous.”

Young represents Cheryl Butler, a black former SMU law professor who says discrimination drove her tenure denial, according to court records. Brown dismissed Butler’s suit in 2023. The Fifth Circuit revived part of it last year.

news.originalContent:
(Photo by AFP via Getty Images)

A luxury world cruise that sold passengers a permanent home at sea abruptly left more than 200 of them stranded in a Cambodian port this week.

The Villa Vie Odyssey was carrying 203 passengers and 156 crew members when its operator suspended the round-the-world voyage in Sihanoukville on Tuesday, according to the Associated Press (AP). Most of those living aboard were Americans.

Chief Executive Kathy Villalba posted the notice to leave shortly after 7:00 a.m., giving residents until 2:00 p.m. to pack and disembark, according to Reuters. Passengers had to arrange their own accommodations, the AP reported.

The company blamed fuel prices that surged after the Iran war began in late February, according to Reuters. Monthly fuel costs for each cabin had climbed from about $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 in parts of Asia, the operator said, and could not shift an increase of that size onto residents. (RELATED: New Iran War Fears Send Oil Past $105 With Diesel Already Sky High)

Residents of the Villa Vie Odyssey cruise ship were left stranded and at a loss in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville after being told to leave the vessel, saying the operator had run out of money to pay for fuel https://t.co/9Ekw1dmlMQ https://t.co/NS18N7Bpzl

Many residents had sold their homes to live aboard full time, according to The Street. “The sudden order to disembark has left many retirees and remote workers homeless thousands of miles from their home countries,” Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province, said in a statement reported by ABC News.

Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, boarded 17 months ago and were repeatedly asked to pay more toward fuel, according to the AP. “We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything,” Lynn Montoya told the AP. Carol Larson, who paid $120,000 for her cabin, voiced no regrets about the investment, the AP reported. “Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk,” Larson said.

The Odyssey set out from Belfast, Northern Ireland, in Oct. 2024 for a planned three-and-a-half-year trip around the globe, according to the AP. It had sailed for at least 755 days before docking in Cambodia, Reuters reported.

Villa Vie had pitched the vessel as a permanent residence, selling lifetime access for a one-time $299,999 for a single cabin or $499,999 for a double, according to Fox Business. The company courted retirees worried about inflation and outliving their savings, Fox Business reported. “For less than the price of an average home, you can secure a lifetime of experiences,” founder Mikael Petterson said in 2024, according to Fox Business.

The ship was set to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, according to Reuters. The company said it would try to restructure and raise new money within 60 days, though it had not secured financing.

news.originalContent:
Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images | Federal Reserve Bank Of Cleveland

Federal Reserve Gov. Lisa Cook and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack broke with their colleagues Wednesday, voting to raise interest rates as the central bank opted to hold borrowing costs steady despite persistent inflation.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to maintain its benchmark interest rate at a range of 3.75% to 4.00%, with Cook and Hammack instead favoring a quarter-percentage-point increase, according to the Fed’s official statement. The dissenting votes underscored disagreements over how aggressively policymakers should respond to rising consumer prices, particularly as elevated energy costs and resilient economic growth complicate efforts to return inflation to the Fed’s 2% target. The split marked Cook’s first dissent as a Fed governor and Hammack’s second since July, when she also supported raising rates to combat inflation. Both officials favored additional monetary tightening Wednesday, while the majority concluded that gathering more economic data before another rate increase was appropriate.

Inflation reached 3.7% annually in September, with gasoline prices rising sharply amid the war with Iran. The Fed’s decision to leave rates unchanged followed September’s quarter-point increase, its first rate hike since 2023, as American households continued to face higher costs for fuel and everyday necessities.

Hammack had repeatedly warned that prolonged inflation could become embedded in the economy, making it harder for the Fed to bring prices under control. In an Oct. 12 speech, she argued that inflationary pressures were spreading beyond individual sectors and that policymakers risked needing more aggressive action if they waited too long.

“With each passing month, persistently elevated inflation raises the risks of an inflationary mindset becoming entrenched in the economy,” Hammack said.

Cook similarly expressed concern about persistent inflation, particularly the effects of higher energy prices and the rapid expansion of artificial intelligence infrastructure. In a Sept. 28 speech, Cook pointed to inflationary pressures from the AI buildout, oil prices and supply chain disruptions associated with the Iran war, while arguing that the labor market remained strong enough to withstand higher borrowing costs.

“This increase was to address inflation, which has been too high for too long,” Cook said of the Fed’s September rate hike.

Cook’s dissent also attracted attention because President Donald Trump has sought to remove her from the Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors over allegations of mortgage fraud, which Cook denies. Trump has repeatedly pushed the central bank to lower interest rates, placing his administration at odds with Cook’s vote Wednesday for an additional increase.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh defended the majority’s decision during Wednesday’s post-meeting press conference, arguing that policymakers needed additional information to determine whether September’s rate increase was having the intended effect.

“If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment, is that what we’ve done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some, but there’s no firm conclusions,” Warsh said.

Warsh acknowledged that inflation remained above the central bank’s target and that rising energy prices continued to burden consumers.

“I’m not going to be the guy who says that oil prices haven’t gone up,” Warsh said.

The Fed’s statement described economic activity as expanding at a “strong pace,” an upgrade from its September assessment, while emphasizing that domestic spending remained resilient and the unemployment rate had changed little. The stronger outlook could give policymakers additional room to raise rates without immediately threatening the Fed’s employment mandate.

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton blasted Democratic rival Xavier Becerra on Thursday for opening the door to a mileage tax that could cost California drivers another $1,000 a year — accusing Democrats of relentlessly gouging working families.

“Now we know that with Xavier Becerra as governor, you’ll pay an extra $1,000 a year just for driving your car,” Hilton told the California Post, just moments before hosting a news conference in the Central Valley town Sanger to discuss a proposal to make gas $3 a gallon.

“They never stop gouging you. First, it’s the highest gas prices in the country, then the highest car registration fees. Now they want to track you everywhere you drive and charge up to 10 cents a mile.”

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

“This is disgusting Democrat elitism at its worst,” Hilton added.

The blistering attack came after Becerra, a former California attorney general and Biden administration health secretary, signaled his willingness to consider taxing motorists for every mile they drive to help pay for the state’s deteriorating roads.

“Everything should be on the table,” Becerra told KCRA’s Ashley Zavala when asked whether he would support a mileage-based tax as governor.

“Our roads aren’t maintained just by some magic wand. We have to pay for it,” Becerra said.

“Do I want to tax people more than necessary? No. Should we pay a gas tax? Yes. Should people who drive electric vehicles, who don’t need gas, pay for those roads to be repaired as well? Absolutely.”

Becerra’s comments handed Hilton a fresh opening just five days before Tuesday’s election, with the Republican making California’s crushing cost of living a centerpiece of his campaign to succeed Gov. Gavin Newsom.

Hilton argued that a mileage tax would disproportionately punish Californians who are already struggling to afford housing, gas for their vehicles and everyday necessities.

“The people who will be hit the hardest are working-class Californians and small business owners who drive their cars and trucks for work — not the work-from-home climate warriors sitting on their laptops lecturing the rest of us about how to live,” Hilton said.

California has spent years studying a mileage-based road charge as an alternative to the gas tax, which transportation officials warn will generate less revenue as motorists increasingly switch to electric and more fuel-efficient vehicles.

The state’s latest pilot program tested charging drivers based on distance traveled, with a final report due to lawmakers by the end of the year.

State Assemblymember Carl DeMaio (R-San Diego) has warned that a potential mileage tax could cost drivers between 6 and 9 cents per mile — on top of existing gasoline and vehicle taxes.

At those rates, a motorist driving 15,000 miles annually could face charges ranging from $900 to $1,350.

Hilton, meanwhile, has promised to dramatically slash the cost of driving in California by lowering gasoline prices to $3 per gallon and capping annual vehicle registration fees at $73.

His proposals include eliminating the state gasoline tax, rolling back environmental regulations and boosting domestic oil production — changes that would require cooperation from California’s Democratic-controlled Legislature.

Hilton said Thursday that he would also block any legislation establishing a mileage tax.

“As governor, I will veto the mileage tax,” he said. “This is just another example of how you’ll save with Steve.”

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

Instadocs: Jane Doe V. Cornell is the latest short film that finds Netflix taking a step toward becoming a news-reporting entity. Arguably, anyway. The streamer that cornered the market on true crime documentaries — be they trashy or credible –—now cranks out “quick turnaround” pieces about hot topics that are ripped from the headlines, with previous entries covering gambling prediction markets, the Alex Murdaugh case and more. The latest addresses a broad problem brought into the light by a high-profile campus sexual assault case.

The Gist: A commentator describes Jane Doe’s lawsuit against Cornell University, filed on Oct. 6, 2026, as being in a “white-hot international spotlight” (thus justifying Netflix’s M.O. for its Instadocs). Sophia Dasser, editor-in-chief of the Cornell Daily Sun, and senior editor Cereese Qusba, tell the story of the unidentified Cornell student who was gang raped in 2024 by members of the Chi Phi fraternity. They describe how the scenario went from consensual to nonconsensual as the survivor was coerced into taking ketamine and the perpetrators advertised their gross misdeeds to 50 people on a Snapchat thread.

The doc then details how Jane Doe reported the incident to campus police and went through procedures outlined by Title IX, the federal civil rights law addressing sexual discrimination on college campuses. Interviewees — including Jane Doe’s lawyer and New York governor Kathy Hochul — maintain that the case wasn’t given the attention it deserved, and some assert that Cornell leadership prioritized maintaining the university’s “good reputation” as an Ivy League school over doing right by Jane Doe.

The story ended up at the top of the news cycle in 2026 after the lawsuit prompted student protests, an apology from Cornell’s president for mishandling the matter, and blanket punishments levied against all fraternities. The incident was emblematic of many similar stories from college campuses in which serious sexual assault crimes result in unserious reprimands against perpetrators. It’s not just a problem at Cornell; it may be a problem with Title IX in general.

What Movies Will It Remind You Of? Kirby Dick’s 2015 doc The Hunting Ground is a piercing criticism of the failure of American universities to adequately deal with sexual assault incidents.

Our Take: Jane Doe V. Cornell is two things: One, a (perhaps surprisingly) journalistically solid encapsulation of a story that dominated recent headlines. It does viewers the service of addressing the primary points of the case with concision, valuable in an era when fragmented news coverage can be overwhelming; it also digs an inch or two deeper than most sources, turning over the Title IX stone to expose the flaws in a system that seems to do more for perpetrators of crimes than for the victims. The nature of the Instadocs format — this one clocks in at 35 minutes — means it doesn’t delve deeper into societal implications or possible solutions to the problem, but the film at the very least puts the voices of real people in the narrative so it’s more than just a glorified Wikipedia article.

But: Two, it leaves us with the generally icky feeling that Netflix circles like a vulture over “controversial” topics, looking for stories to exploit for streaming views — and Jane Doe V. Cornell covers the most sensitive topic in the series yet. Although interviews with assault survivors are handled delicately, and the use of female voices gives the doc some credibility, the subtext is nevertheless troubling. By its very nature, the series’ stomp-on-the-gas production turnaround and the narrative limitations therein undermines the definition of documentary filmmaking. (Quick aside to documentary filmmakers: Please stop interviewing lawyers who aren’t public servants — their commentary is too often worthless.) This Instadoc isn’t far removed from a longer news story we’d see on CNN, with all the positives and negatives inherent therein.

Our Call: Please note the criticisms of the Instadocs concept in general as we give a tepid STREAM IT to Jane Doe V. Cornell for how it clears some of the news-cycle clutter to deliver a decent-enough overview of a complex story.

John Serba is a freelance film critic from Grand Rapids, Michigan. Werner Herzog hugged him once.

James Madison’s College Football Playoff (CFP) hopes took a huge hit last week with a loss to Appalachian State, but the Dukes (7-1, 4-1 Sun Belt) have no time to lick their wounds.

If James Madison is going to resurrect its season, it will need a bounce-back effort against Troy on Thursday night.

It’s not just about winning out for the Dukes, but they must do it in style if they’re going to get the attention of the Selection Committee.

Thursday offers an opportunity to do just that with James Madison installed as a 21-point favorite over the Trojans at Bridgeforth Stadium.

The loss to Appalachian State may be too much to ignore in terms of the CFP, but it doesn’t change the fact that James Madison is one of the best teams in the Group of 6.

The Dukes are the highest-ranked (No. 29) G6 team in Bill Connelly’s SP+ power rankings, and they are the third-highest behind Boise State and New Mexico in Sagarin (No. 60).

The committee does take those factors into account when it comes time to hand out tickets to the big dance, but the Dukes will need to back up those lofty rankings with results.

Speaking of those rankings, no team in FBS had a lower one than Louisiana-Monroe before Week 7. Why does that matter? Because the Warhawks just earned their first win of the season (leaving Northern Illinois as the only team without a win in the country) over Troy. The Trojans were up 14-3, at home, with three minutes left in the fourth quarter before all hell broke loose.

It may be tough for James Madison to pick themselves up off the mat after a season-crushing loss, but it pales in comparison to what will be lingering in the Troy locker room.

And it’s not just the lack of wind in their sails that makes Troy cannon fodder for the Dukes on Thursday. The numbers paint this one as a mismatch, especially since Trojans QB Goose Crowder has been dealing with a shoulder injury, which has severely limited his output.

The senior signal-caller is just 15-for-30 for 115 yards with one interception over his last two outings.

Troy’s offense, which ranks outside the top 100 in both points per game and yards per play, will have quite a difficult time keeping up with James Madison, which is highly incentivized to run this score up.

The Play: James Madison -21 (-110, DraftKings)

news.originalContent:
See more of our coverage in your search results.

The Raiders have given Jackson Powers-Johnson and Caleb Rogers ample opportunities to take command at right guard.

Neither has done enough to keep the Raiders from looking for someone else.

Now, rookie Trey Zuhn III appears to be getting his chance.

Zuhn was spotted alongside the other starters during a practice drill Wednesday, a potential indication that the Raiders are leaning toward giving him his first NFL start Sunday against the Jets. While no starting assignment has been publicly confirmed, his placement offered a telling clue about the direction of their latest offensive line shakeup.

And after Rogers endured a particularly rough afternoon against the Rams, there is plenty of reason to consider another option.

“We’re going to give other guys opportunities,” coach Klint Kubiak said of the offensive line in general. “We’re going to keep shaking it up until we find the right mix.”

The Raiders are still searching.

Powers-Johnson and Rogers have not taken command at right guard, leaving the Raiders with an unsettled situation where they desperately need dependable play.

Rogers’ struggles against the Rams only reinforced the concern.

The problems extend beyond one position, but the inability to get consistent production at right guard has contributed to a feeble running game that continues to undermine the offense. Too often, the Raiders have been pushed around inside rather than creating the room their backs need.

That has helped result in the Raiders fielding the NFL’s third-worst rushing attack.

During a four-game losing streak, that weakness has become increasingly difficult to overlook.

Turning to Zuhn would represent another attempt to address it.

“I feel confident,” Zuhn said of his ability to step in at guard after also practicing at tackle and center this year. “If that’s what the team needs, it’s what I’m ready to do.

“I’ve just been taking every rep I can at practice doing whatever the team needs me. I’m happy to take them because I’m just trying to get on the field and help the team.”

His preparation has required flexibility.

Rather than concentrating exclusively on one position, Zuhn has worked to make himself useful across the line. That versatility gives the Raiders options, although their most immediate need is finding a combination capable of executing consistently.

As Kubiak said this week, Zuhn is a “Swiss Army knife.”

“He can do it all. He can play tackle, guard, center. He might be able to play quarterback,” Kubiak said. “I don’t know, I haven’t let him try yet.”

For now, he’ll probably stick to trying to protect the quarterback.

And helping open running lanes would be a welcome addition.

“He’s a very intelligent, hardworking player who’s still ascending and still getting better,” Kubiak said. “He’ll have his chance.”

Zuhn has approached the wait as an opportunity to learn.

Veteran center Tyler Linderbaum and left tackle Kolton Miller have provided examples to study, with Zuhn paying attention to the small technical details that can determine whether a blocker wins or loses an assignment.

“I’ve been learning so much, especially with all the vets in the room like Tyler and Kolton,” he said. “I’ve just been learning from them and all the coaches, trying to be a sponge and learn whatever I can, especially the little details like hand placement, foot speed, foot placement. Just steps. There’s so much you can learn from watching them.”

The next step could be putting those lessons to work.

Starting a rookie would come with its own uncertainty, and Zuhn alone cannot repair everything wrong with the Raiders’ running game. But the extended auditions for Powers-Johnson and Rogers have not produced a firm answer at right guard.

At some point, giving another player an opportunity becomes the logical response.

Wednesday’s practice suggested the Raiders could be approaching that point with Zuhn.

They have spent weeks waiting for someone to take ownership of the position. Their latest adjustment could give the rookie a chance to do it.

The ex-wife of Jason Galanis, Savannah Chrisley’s fraudster fiancé, begged for him to receive a lenient prison sentence by painting him as an animal lover.

In a July 2017 sentencing memorandum obtained exclusively by Page Six, Galanis’ then-wife, Monet Berger, shared a story about how her then-husband once rescued an injured hawk as a way to vouch for his character.

“He also has a love of animals like no other,” Berger, 57, told the Manhattan federal judge overseeing Galanis’ fraud case.

“A few years ago, we were driving home from dinner, and he saw a hawk on the side of the road,” Berger wrote. “When we got home, he insisted on going back to see if it was injured.”

Berger said Galanis, 56, put the bird in their car and brought it back to their house, where he “made a bed for it with blankets.”

Galanis then “found the hawk [a] rescue facility, which was 90 minutes away, and drove the hawk there at night so it could get proper care,” according to Berger.

She further claimed he “monitored” the hawk “daily” and “made a donation” to the rescue facility.

Elsewhere in the letter, Berger explained she’d spent “the past 20 years by [Galanis’] side as his life partner.”

She described him as a “loyal” and “loving” man who supported her during her “health issues,” was a “friend to all” and would often “help a stranger.”

Berger also echoed many of the arguments Galanis and his defense team made in their own pleas for leniency, including that his career criminal father, John Galanis, had had a lasting “painful impact” on his eldest son and “destroyed” his life.

While John was in federal prison for financial crimes, Berger claimed Jason “was forced to drop out of [college]” and “give up his own dreams and his own life to become a caretaker to his younger brothers and his mother for his entire life.”

Berger further claimed John “seemed to have some spell” on Jason and “had such a hold over” him that he “did not stand a chance against him,” adding that John “used his four sons as human shields throughout their lives with no regard [for] the damage and harm he has inflicted upon them.”

Berger wondered whether “counseling” to address Jason’s “issues with his father” would have led to a different trajectory for him.

“Jason has made mistakes, and he knows that,” Berger penned, insisting he “has such regrets.”

“I am begging you to please consider the mental hardships he was under due to this unhealthy relationship his father imposed on him,” she told the judge.

“Jason knows what he did was wrong and the gravity of the crime. His father was out of his life for many years, and somehow he manipulated his way back into Jason’s life.”

In September 2020, Jason was sentenced to 189 months behind bars after pleading guilty to seven felonies: three counts of conspiracy to commit securities fraud, two counts of securities fraud one count of investment adviser fraud and one count of conspiracy to commit investment adviser fraud.

Notably, John was one of his co-defendants.

Berger went on to highlight Jason’s years-long work with Operation Gratitude, a nonprofit that supports deployed troops, veterans, law enforcement, first responders and their families.

She argued that the charitable “side” of Jason — which “is who [he] is” — “was not allowed to be developed when he was younger” due to his “family influence.”

Sign up for Virtual Reali-Tea with Danny and Evan, our must-read newsletter!

Please provide a valid email.

By clicking above you agree to the Terms of Use and Privacy Policy.

Want more celebrity and pop culture news?

Berger concluded her “request to consider leniency” by branding Jason a “kind,” “caring” and “hardworking man who cares about others’ well-being.”

She added, “His business life might be finished due to these mistakes, but he has much to offer the community through his service and kindness and compassion for people.”

Just one month later, Berger filed for divorce, citing “irreconcilable differences.” Interestingly, she listed their date of separation as May 23, 2016.

Berger explained in her petition that she was unaware Jason had allegedly underpaid or failed to pay taxes on his income and allegedly forged her signature on more than one tax document, describing herself as a victim of his crimes.

The exes finalized their split in April 2018.

Jason and his fiancée’s fraudster dad, Todd Chrisley — who is only one year older than his soon-to-be son-in-law — actually served time together.

In March 2025, President Donald Trump commuted Jason’s prison sentence. Two months later, he pardoned Savannah’s parents — Todd and his wife, Julie Chrisley — too.

On her podcast Tuesday, Savannah, 29, revealed she’d met her “much-older” man in the “world of politics” and that he proposed to her in the Cayman Islands in December 2025 after almost two years of dating.

The “Chrisley Knows Best” alum — who lives with Jason in her newly purchased Nashville home — also announced the couple is expecting their first child together.

news.originalContent:
Palestinian voters could decide Israel’s future, but its political class refuses to accept their mandate.

Few certainties have emerged from Israel’s parliamentary elections. The diverse coalition of Israel’s self-styled ‘Zionist’ opposition remains short of a majority. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud appears to be the largest party, but its electoral bloc has not secured enough seats to form a government.

What is not in doubt, however, is the surge in turnout from Palestinian citizens of Israel, which has established Arab parties as a pivotal bloc in the parliament, potentially one able to determine which of the rival camps forms a government, if either is willing to work with them.

Anger over Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, and what analysts have described as the overt racism of its governing coalition helped drive Palestinian citizens of Israel to the polls in large numbers.

An estimated 80 percent of eligible Palestinian voters in Israel turned out for Tuesday’s election, marking a surge in participation by a community that accounts for about 21 percent of the population.

The turnout has given the two main electoral lists representing Palestinian citizens of Israel – the United Arab List (Ra’am) and the Joint List – a combined 19 seats in the 120-member parliament, potentially giving them a decisive role in determining who forms the next government.

However, rather than acknowledge that groundswell of support, Israel’s leading politicians have sought to either delegitimise their vote – attributing it to foreign interference – or somehow cast Palestinians exercising their democratic right as an “attempt to steal the election”.

Framing the result as a bid to secure the “Islamisation of Israel”, Netanyahu’s ruling Likud party has gone so far as to call on Israel’s internal security service, the Shin Bet, to investigate the possibility of foreign election interference into the large-scale Palestinian turnout. In doing so, they appear to have thrown the legitimacy of the Arab vote into question and tainted any future attempt by the opposition to ally with the Arab parties.

Despite denouncing Netanyahu’s government as corrupt, incompetent and damaging to Israel’s international standing, much of Israel’s Jewish-led opposition has remained reluctant to embrace the support of Palestinian parties to remove him from power.

The left-wing Democrats have been the likeliest to cooperate with the Palestinian parties, while other opposition figures have either resisted such an alliance or stopped short of rejecting allegations that foreign actors helped engineer the surge in Palestinian voter turnout.

On election night, former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid ruled out sitting alongside Palestinian parties in government, despite having relied on their support during their brief 2021–22 government.

On Thursday, another leading member of the opposition, Avigdor Lieberman, the hard-right leader of Yisrael Beytenu, also ruled out forming a coalition with Palestinian parties. He said he would sit alongside “neither Bibi nor Tibi”, using Netanyahu’s established nickname and invoking Ahmad Tibi, leader of the Ta’al party – part of the Joint List – as a stand-in for the wider Palestinian bloc.

“It was clear from campaigning that there was going to be a large turnout,” said Orly Noy, who stood for the Palestinian-dominated Balad party. “The [governing] coalition had shown there were no red lines in Gaza and Palestinians in Israel sensed they might be next. People also just couldn’t face another term of soaring crime and a police force headed by [far-right National Security Minister] Itamar Ben-Gvir.”

“What few rights Palestinians had have been slipping away since October 7. The last tool they had in their toolbox – the only thing they had that was equal to everyone else – was their vote, so they used that in massive numbers, but even that now seems to be being undermined and delegitimised,” she said.

news.originalContent:
Army Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia was subject of investigation into leaking information about Iran and Ukraine.

Hegseth cuts US generals and admirals by 20%, launches autonomous warfare command

United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has fired the director of the Strategy, Plans and Policy Directorate at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Lieutenant General Brett Sylvia, for what the Pentagon says is severe misconduct. The move comes amid reports that the US had warned its allies of a possible renewal of strikes against Iran.

A Department of Defense official told Al Jazeera on Thursday that Sylvia had been “meeting with journalists outside the Pentagon in order to leak classified information”.

“Sylvia is the subject of an investigation for leaking classified information about the Iran war, the war between Russia and Ukraine, and more,” the official added.

The investigation into Sylvia remains ongoing and has been referred to the Department of Justice for further action, according to the Pentagon.

The official said Sylvia was the Defense Department’s chief military planner but “was not a central planner for the Iran war”. “That is the responsibility of CENTCOM [Central Command] and its commander, Admiral [Brad] Cooper,” the official said.

Sylvia’s firing comes as Trump has repeatedly floated starting new military operations against Iran.

He is the second person to be ousted from the post, known in military circles as the J5, under Hegseth. His predecessor was forced to retire in October last year.

“Sylvia failed three polygraphs which questioned him about leaking classified information,” the Pentagon official said while accusing Sylvia of putting national security at risk.

“Urgent action was needed and could not wait another second,” he concluded.

There is no immediate replacement for Sylvia, according to an official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to The Associated Press news agency.

Before arriving at the Joint Chiefs of Staff, Sylvia served as commander of the 101st Airborne Division at Fort Campbell, Kentucky, until May 2025, according to his official biography, which has now been taken offline. He also previously served as the vice director for the office he recently led.

His military awards include six Bronze Star Medals, including one for valour, and a Purple Heart, indicating he was wounded in combat.

Sean Parnel, assistant to the defense secretary for public affairs, said earlier on Thursday in a post on X that “the Department of War has zero tolerance for the intentional, unauthorized disclosure of classified information.” He did not refer specifically to Sylvia.

Sylvia is the latest senior Pentagon official whom Hegseth has accused of leaking to the media. He fired three aides from his inner circle last year as part of a broader leak investigation that included polygraph tests.

President Donald Trump has promised to “finish the job” in Iran after launching the war with Israel eight months ago and said he would do so after the midterm elections on Tuesday.

news.originalContent:
Republicans in a Texas county have filed a lawsuit asking for ballots in the state’s midterm races to be hand-counted.

Days before the United States’ pivotal midterm elections, a Texas group affiliated with the Republican Party has asked a federal judge to stop certification of the state’s upcoming election results.

In a lawsuit filed on Tuesday, the Potter County Republican Party and its chairman, Daniel Rogers, claim potential election interference by artificial intelligence (AI) or “malicious actors” that could compromise the results of next Tuesday’s elections in Texas.

The plaintiffs, who are asking for a hand count of every ballot from every precinct in the state before election certification happens, allege voting machines have components inside made by China that would allow them to be manipulated.

“If a component is tampered with during manufacturing, it could serve as a point of entry for unlawful and malfeasance hackers, allowing for the possibility of synchronized attacks across multiple election machines and jurisdictions,” the lawsuit read.

The legal challenge comes as several polls show Democrat James Talarico narrowly leading his Republican challenger, Ken Paxton, in Texas’ all-important US Senate race that could ultimately decide which party controls the chamber after November 3.

The Talarico and Paxton campaigns and the Potter County Republican Party did not immediately return requests from Al Jazeera for comment.

The legal complaint does not specify if any voting machines in Potter County, or elsewhere in Texas, have been compromised. The plaintiffs acknowledged in their filing that no previous election in the county was “altered” by a third party, arguing that the possibility of vote manipulation by AI makes the state’s election safeguards easily compromised.

“The real likelihood of a clever and undetected hack by recently developed AI programs, which conceal their activity to avoid detection, reinforces the need for a full verification based on hand-counting of all paper records or ballots in all Texas precincts, prior to certification of the federal results,” they wrote.

State law in Texas already requires hand-count audits in elections where electronic tabulators are used. But the plaintiffs argue that does not go far enough.

“The paper record or ballot provides an independent verification mechanism only if election officials actually compare a complete hand count of all of the paper records or ballots,” the filing said.

The lawsuit also claims US “adversaries”, such as China, Iran and Russia, are capable of accessing election systems.

US President Donald Trump in July declassified documents that, he claimed, showed Chinese interference in the US 2020 presidential election, reviving his attacks on US elections despite no evidence that Beijing impacted the vote he lost that year.

Last week, the US Department of Justice also sought to block certification of an election, claiming, in Alaska, that an independent candidate with the same name as the state’s Republican Senator up for re-election is running in order to mislead voters.

Alicia Pierce, a spokeswoman for Texas’s Secretary of State, whose office administers elections in the state, said it “does not plan to comment on the lawsuit at this time”.

news.originalContent:
Muslim advocates say the best way to respond to hate is to elect the Democratic candidate in Michigan to US Senate.

Al Jazeera speaks to El-Sayed as religion becomes flashpoint in Senate race

Dearborn, Michigan – Jake Lang, a far-right provocateur in a bulletproof vest, shouts anti-Muslim obscenities on a bullhorn outside a rally featuring former US President Barack Obama in Detroit.

His associates, wearing crusader-themed accessories – including a tin shield featuring a black cross – hold campaign signs for Mike Rogers, the Republican Senate candidate in Michigan, who is in a close race with Democrat Abdul El-Sayed.

If it weren’t for the bigoted slogans, the people lining up around them to attend the campaign event for El-Sayed and other Democrats could have mistakenly thought the protesters were in Halloween costumes.

“Get the f*** out, Muslims,” Lang shouted. “The crusade is coming. Self-deport.”

Lang may appear like a fringe agitator. But Muslim American activists say the bigotry he is spreading is going mainstream, especially in the context of the Senate race in Michigan.

Anti-Muslim attacks against El-Sayed have been perpetuated at the highest level of the US government, including by President Donald Trump and his cabinet members.

Suehaila Amen, a prominent Arab and Muslim advocate in the Detroit area, said bigotry against her community is reaching an all-time high.

“They make immediately post 9/11 look like a walk in the park for us. This has been absolutely disgusting to witness,” Amen told Al Jazeera.

One of Lang’s allies, Pastor Lorenzo Sewell, is an official faith adviser to the Rogers campaign.

Sewell helped Lang organise an anti-Muslim march in the Detroit suburb of Dearborn – home to a large Arab and Muslim community – in August.

Abdullah Hammoud, the mayor of Dearborn, said the city – which has long been a target for anti-Muslim provocateurs – has been receiving an increased number of threats in recent months.

“The general public is unaware of how many threats are aimed towards the city of Dearborn on a daily basis, via social [media], via our dispatch when they’re calling 911 or calling our call centre, and lobbing these threats against the residents of the city each and every single day,” Hammoud told Al Jazeera.

While the Rogers campaign did not respond to Al Jazeera’s request for comment about the Republican candidate’s links to Sewell, Rogers defended his focus on El-Sayed’s background, saying it was for national security.

“This is not about the way you pray; it’s the way you think,” Rogers told reporters after his debate with El-Sayed earlier this month.

Local leaders say their community is not cowering in the face of such threats and Trump’s near-daily attacks, and is pushing back through civic engagement and rallying around the El-Sayed campaign.

“Trump is a fascist,” Hammoud told Al Jazeera. “I think the best thing we can do, the best response, is to send Abdul to the US Senate, somebody who’s got two doctorates, someone who is a son of this country, a son of the state, someone who is the captain of his high school team … I think that that’s the best response that we can give fascism.”

Trump has repeatedly mocked El-Sayed’s name, misrepresenting it as Mohammed, and called the Democratic candidate a “jihadist”.

Amen said Arab and Muslim Americans are used to being targeted for their names, but when the president does it, it legitimises bigotry and racism.

“It’s not just some loser that lives around the block who may call you a racist expletive; it’s the loser who lives in the White House,” she said.

Amen added that Arab and Muslim communities are going about their daily lives and organising politically despite the escalating attacks, stressing that they reject attempts to cast them as foreigners or outsiders.

“We are an integral part of the fabric of this nation, whether people like it or not,” she told Al Jazeera.

As the Senate race intensifies, Rogers has been baselessly accusing El-Sayed of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Last month, Rogers went as far as agreeing with a social media post calling El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official, a “terrorist”.

Trump has suggested that El-Sayed would be a physical threat to the Capitol, saying that he would want him to go through a metal detector.

At an event in western Michigan earlier this week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr incorrectly claimed that Arabs do not produce literature or science and “don’t win Nobel Prizes”. He argued that the Muslim Brotherhood – which only briefly held power in Egypt between 2012 and 2013 – has destroyed Arab civilisation.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz joined in on such attacks, describing El-Sayed as a “jihadist leprechaun”.

Cruz warned that El-Sayed, a Michigan-born and raised father of two with a medical degree and a doctorate in public health, could end up on the Senate Intelligence Committee and endanger national security.

“If I am correct that he is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result,” he said.

On Wednesday, Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy invoked Dearborn – one of the safest and fastest-growing cities in Michigan – to drum up fear of immigration.

“Look at what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan, for God’s sake. We’re not going to let that come to our state of Ohio,” he said.

El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent, has avoided focusing on the attacks, calling them “deflections and deceptions”.

It’s not clear how attacks linked to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and Arab heritage will affect the race.

About 38 percent of respondents in a survey of potential voters conducted by Michigan State University said a candidate being a Muslim would make them less likely to offer support to their campaign.

After a Trump rally for Rogers in Port Huron, northeast of Detroit, where the president spent most of his nearly two-hour speech attacking El-Sayed, some attendees appeared to agree that El-Sayed may be a threat to national security.

As the US president spoke, shouts of “traitor”, referring to El-Sayed, erupted from the crowd.

Trump supporter David Beamer, whose son died in the 9/11 attacks in 2001, spoke at the event and questioned El-Sayed’s American identity.

“Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American,” Beamer said.

Al Jazeera asked Duane Crempa, a 72-year-old Republican in a Batman mask who attended the Trump speech on Sunday, whether he believes that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” as Trump claims.

Crempa said he is a good judge of character. “Yeah, there is something not right with him. That’s all I’ll say; there’s definitely something not right,” he added.

Jermaine Miller, who also was at the rally, told Al Jazeera he hopes El-Sayed is not a “terrorist”.

“But I mean, it sounds convincing, but it is believable,” he said of Trump’s allegations that the Democratic candidate is a “jihadist”.

In the Detroit area, Arab and Muslim advocates say the issue is bigger than a Senate seat, arguing that such rhetoric endangers their communities and risks ripping the social fabric of the state.

“We’ve seen the increase in hate marches and hate speech and people being very comfortable sharing their hateful views online and coming into our city and harassing people for no reason – people who are just trying to live and function in this country,” Amen said.

“It’s been tremendously heartbreaking to watch our community constantly have to question why people are maliciously maligning them in public.”

Earlier this year, two gunmen killed three people outside a mosque complex in San Diego in southern California in what authorities said was a hate crime.

Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, who represents Dearborn and parts of Detroit, said she fears for her two Muslim boys, Adam and Yousif, amid the rise of hate with the election campaign.

“Yesterday, we were all watching the football game, and we literally had to turn off the ads every time in between [plays] because we didn’t want our babies to see these awful, racist ads,” Tlaib told Al Jazeera.

“It’s awful to live this way right now.”

With petrol in Michigan nearing record highs, Arab and Muslim advocates say their communities are being scapegoated to cover up the shortcomings of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran.

Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), said the attacks against El-Sayed amount to “disgusting Islamophobia” that serves as a distraction.

“Abdul El-Sayed’s name is a visibly Muslim name, and it’s being treated as inherently suspicious, as if a Muslim American cannot willfully execute their duties as an active member of Congress to protect the American people,” Abdelrahman told Al Jazeera.

At the Trump rally in Port Huron, one of Trump’s allies appeared to weigh El-Sayed’s candidacy against petrol prices.

Brian Pannebecker, a retiree from an auto manufacturing company Trump invited to the stage on Sunday, stressed that Michiganders need to vote for the Republican ticket.

“I don’t care if they’re paying a buck and a half more a gallon for gasoline. That is no excuse to vote for a socialist Islamist for the US Senate,” Pannebecker said.

Amen said Arab and Muslim Americans are used to being targeted for their names, but when the president does it, it legitimises bigotry and racism.

“It’s not just some loser that lives around the block who may call you a racist expletive; it’s the loser who lives in the White House,” she said.

Amen added that Arab and Muslim communities are going about their daily lives and organising politically despite the escalating attacks, stressing that they reject attempts to cast them as foreigners or outsiders.

“We are an integral part of the fabric of this nation, whether people like it or not,” she told Al Jazeera.

As the Senate race intensifies, Rogers has been baselessly accusing El-Sayed of ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran.

Last month, Rogers went as far as agreeing with a social media post calling El-Sayed, a doctor and former public health official, a “terrorist”.

Trump has suggested that El-Sayed would be a physical threat to the Capitol, saying that he would want him to go through a metal detector.

At an event in western Michigan earlier this week, Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr incorrectly claimed that Arabs do not produce literature or science and “don’t win Nobel Prizes”. He argued that the Muslim Brotherhood – which only briefly held power in Egypt between 2012 and 2013 – has destroyed Arab civilisation.

Texas Senator Ted Cruz joined in on such attacks, describing El-Sayed as a “jihadist leprechaun”.

Cruz warned that El-Sayed, a Michigan-born and raised father of two with a medical degree and a doctorate in public health, could end up on the Senate Intelligence Committee and endanger national security.

“If I am correct that he is a passionate supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, there is a very real risk that Americans will die as a result,” he said.

On Wednesday, Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy invoked Dearborn – one of the safest and fastest-growing cities in Michigan – to drum up fear of immigration.

“Look at what’s happening in Dearborn, Michigan, for God’s sake. We’re not going to let that come to our state of Ohio,” he said.

El-Sayed, who is of Egyptian descent, has avoided focusing on the attacks, calling them “deflections and deceptions”.

It’s not clear how attacks linked to El-Sayed’s Muslim faith and Arab heritage will affect the race.

About 38 percent of respondents in a survey of potential voters conducted by Michigan State University said a candidate being a Muslim would make them less likely to offer support to their campaign.

After a Trump rally for Rogers in Port Huron, northeast of Detroit, where the president spent most of his nearly two-hour speech attacking El-Sayed, some attendees appeared to agree that El-Sayed may be a threat to national security.

As the US president spoke, shouts of “traitor”, referring to El-Sayed, erupted from the crowd.

Trump supporter David Beamer, whose son died in the 9/11 attacks in 2001, spoke at the event and questioned El-Sayed’s American identity.

“Abdul has a birth certificate. The birth certificate says he’s a citizen of America. You know what? A birth certificate doesn’t make you an American,” Beamer said.

Al Jazeera asked Duane Crempa, a 72-year-old Republican in a Batman mask who attended the Trump speech on Sunday, whether he believes that El-Sayed is a “jihadist” as Trump claims.

Crempa said he is a good judge of character. “Yeah, there is something not right with him. That’s all I’ll say; there’s definitely something not right,” he added.

Jermaine Miller, who also was at the rally, told Al Jazeera he hopes El-Sayed is not a “terrorist”.

“But I mean, it sounds convincing, but it is believable,” he said of Trump’s allegations that the Democratic candidate is a “jihadist”.

In the Detroit area, Arab and Muslim advocates say the issue is bigger than a Senate seat, arguing that such rhetoric endangers their communities and risks ripping the social fabric of the state.

“We’ve seen the increase in hate marches and hate speech and people being very comfortable sharing their hateful views online and coming into our city and harassing people for no reason – people who are just trying to live and function in this country,” Amen said.

“It’s been tremendously heartbreaking to watch our community constantly have to question why people are maliciously maligning them in public.”

Earlier this year, two gunmen killed three people outside a mosque complex in San Diego in southern California in what authorities said was a hate crime.

Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib, who represents Dearborn and parts of Detroit, said she fears for her two Muslim boys, Adam and Yousif, amid the rise of hate with the election campaign.

“Yesterday, we were all watching the football game, and we literally had to turn off the ads every time in between [plays] because we didn’t want our babies to see these awful, racist ads,” Tlaib told Al Jazeera.

“It’s awful to live this way right now.”

With petrol in Michigan nearing record highs, Arab and Muslim advocates say their communities are being scapegoated to cover up the shortcomings of the Trump administration, including the war in Iran.

Abdelhalim Abdelrahman, communication director for American Muslims for Palestine (AMP), said the attacks against El-Sayed amount to “disgusting Islamophobia” that serves as a distraction.

“Abdul El-Sayed’s name is a visibly Muslim name, and it’s being treated as inherently suspicious, as if a Muslim American cannot willfully execute their duties as an active member of Congress to protect the American people,” Abdelrahman told Al Jazeera.

At the Trump rally in Port Huron, one of Trump’s allies appeared to weigh El-Sayed’s candidacy against petrol prices.

Brian Pannebecker, a retiree from an auto manufacturing company Trump invited to the stage on Sunday, stressed that Michiganders need to vote for the Republican ticket.

“I don’t care if they’re paying a buck and a half more a gallon for gasoline. That is no excuse to vote for a socialist Islamist for the US Senate,” Pannebecker said.

news.originalContent:
The US tech giant is investing $15bn in a huge new data centre project in northern Finland.

Finnish police have launched a criminal investigation into suspected breaches of environmental law at the construction site of a planned Google data centre in northern Finland.

The project is part of a $15bn deal announced last month by Alphabet’s Google to invest in artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure in Finland, which the US company described as its largest investment in Europe.

Authorities have said Tuike Finland, a local subsidiary of Google, conducted forest clearing and drainage at a planned site near the town of Muhos, before the environmental impact assessments required under Finnish law had been completed.

“We are investigating whether the company’s operations have breached the Water Act and resulted in environmental damage,” Detective Superintendent Kari Pakanen told the Reuters news agency on Thursday, adding that a guilty finding could lead to a corporate fine.

Pakanen declined to say whether any individuals could become a target of the investigation, and a Google spokesperson said the company would cooperate with the police investigation and continue to focus on maintaining compliance at its sites.

Videos and photographs showing the scale of the forest clearance at the site of the data centre, and Google’s initial reluctance to address the issue in the days after the news broke, have prompted widespread anger in Finland, where there is a high level of respect for the natural environment among the public.

“All the outrage and dismay directed at Google, I can very much share that, especially when we are talking about the parent company valued as the third-largest in the world,” Finnish Green MP Oras Tynkkynen told Al Jazeera. “There is just no excuse. You have to know the legislation of the country you are operating in; you can afford to hire the best legal experts to help you navigate the local legal requirements.”

Finnish authorities ordered Google to stop work at the data centre site at the start of October, and the latest information from the police highlights shortcomings in the drainage and water management at the site.

Tynkkynen called Google’s actions “unforgivable”, but cautioned that while the anger being directed at the US tech giant was justified, it was also diverting scrutiny away from legacy Finnish forestry companies, which he says are “by far the biggest contributors to biodiversity loss in this country”.

Finland’s cool climate, low-carbon electricity and government endorsement of AI projects have contributed to making the country one of Europe’s main destinations for data centre investments in recent years.

Finland, similar in size to Germany – but with one-seventh of the population, less than six million people – has had less vocal opposition to data centre buildouts than other places, including in the United States.

AI data centres are among the main drivers of a projected rise of up to 40 percent in Finland’s electricity consumption in the coming years, if all agreed grid connection projects go ahead, grid operator Fingrid has said.

Google’s planned investments in Finland include data centres, electricity grid improvements and clean energy and battery projects to power services such as Gemini, Search, Maps and YouTube.

Supporting Google’s plan, Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said in September that the deal would be a boost for the economy, playing down concerns that it would suck up energy and push up power prices.

news.originalContent:
Marking three decades, Al Jazeera unveils a new structure: three channels, 33 programmes, and tech-driven innovation.

Al Jazeera is marking its 30-year anniversary with a transformation of the network, introducing a three-channel structure for its Arabic-language broadcasting operation and 33 programmes aimed at providing audiences with more in-depth coverage and analysis.

Since its launch on November 1, 1996, the Qatar-based network has helped reshape Arab journalism, challenging dominant political narratives and providing a platform for political debate rarely seen on television in the region at the time.

Reflecting on this enduring legacy during a special anniversary episode of the network’s Arabic-language Baad al-Bath podcast, veteran anchor Khadija Benguenna detailed the foundational shifts the network brought to the Arab news industry.

Benguenna said that Al Jazeera had popularised practices such as breaking news alerts, continuous live coverage, and exclusive reporting, which were subsequently adopted by other Arab broadcasters.

Former Al Jazeera news director Ahmad al-Sheikh echoed that sentiment during his appearance on the same broadcast. He described the Arab world’s media environment as previously devoid of independent voices, and credited Al Jazeera with providing an example for other Arab broadcasters to improve standards across the board.

The anniversary brings a significant restructuring of the Al Jazeera Media Network’s Arabic-language news services, separating rolling breaking news coverage, live event broadcasting, and more in-depth reporting across three channels.

Speaking to the Qatari newspaper Al Raya, Asef Hamidi, the managing director of Al Jazeera Arabic, described the changes as a “new renaissance” for Al Jazeera. “We are talking about numerous paths undergoing significant development that the audience will notice,” Hamidi said.

Hamidi, who was appointed to his current position in September 2025, said the restructuring was intended to address the growing volume and complexity of news and the need to offer audiences different ways of following events.

In an interview with Qatari newspaper Al Watan, Sheikh Nasser bin Faisal Al Thani, Al Jazeera Media Network director general, explained the philosophical necessity behind the expansion.

“From the very beginning, Al Jazeera was more than just another television channel,” Sheikh Nasser said. “It was a broader project to deepen public understanding.”

He said the strategy for the network’s fourth decade would be guided by three principles.

“Our fourth decade will be defined by three priorities: immediacy, understanding and the human dimension,” he said.

Under the new structure, each of Al Jazeera’s three Arabic-language news channels will have a distinct editorial focus.

Al Jazeera Mubasher, which began broadcasting in 2005, will continue its concentration on uninterrupted live coverage of events, without commentary from presenters or correspondents.

For breaking developments, the new Al Jazeera Now service will focus on developments as they unfold. But unlike a conventional news channel, it will operate without scheduled bulletins or a fixed programme grid.

Meanwhile, the flagship Al Jazeera Arabic channel will retain its news bulletins while pivoting more towards in-depth analysis and investigative journalism, as well as other programmes.

The restructuring is accompanied by plans for 33 programmes, promoted under the slogan “Your questions are our questions”.

Sheikh Nasser said the expansion was intended to provide more context on news events to Arab viewers.

“The real competitor today is not another channel, but noise – the flood of information that makes understanding harder, not easier,” he said, adding that Al Jazeera wanted to fill that gap in understanding.

Hamidi said the new programming would include investigative documentaries, discussions of political and social issues, and programmes examining the historical roots of current conflicts.

The network’s ambitions extend beyond television broadcasting to strengthening Al Jazeera’s local and regional reporting through dedicated digital platforms covering Palestine, Egypt, Sudan, the Gulf and other parts of the Arab world.

The Syria Now platform, which offers documentaries, investigations, and field reporting focused on Syrian affairs, has quickly emerged as one of the primary digital outlets for news on the country.

Looking ahead, the network is also planning a project called Al Jazeera Cultural, provisionally scheduled for launch in late 2027.

The initiative will serve as a space to foster sustained debate about the Arab world’s cultural and intellectual life.

The expansion also forms part of a wider technological transformation, including the development of The Core, an artificial intelligence initiative announced in December 2025 in collaboration with Google Cloud.

The initiative aims to integrate AI into newsroom operations, helping journalists manage information, coordinate coverage and make better use of the network’s reporting archives.

One component, Orbit, is being designed to coordinate newsroom workflows, including monitoring developments, commissioning stories, organising interviews, translating material and managing reporting assignments.

Sheikh Nasser said the first phase of The Core is scheduled to launch on November 1.

Despite the increased use of AI, Sheikh Nasser insisted that human oversight would remain primary.

“Artificial intelligence enables the human and does not replace him,” Sheikh Nasser said. “The main standard for us is conscience and editorial judgement, and editorial judgement is human.”

news.originalContent:
Opposition lawmakers disrupt parliament session, accusing the prime minister of downplaying ongoing antigovernment protests.

The leader of Albania’s opposition has branded members of the government as “criminals”, while he and fellow lawmakers disrupted a parliamentary session by setting off flares and smoke bombs.

Sali Berisha and other opposition members stormed parliament in the capital, Tirana, on Thursday in support of demonstrators, who are demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama’s resignation. Berisha and his colleagues unsuccessfully tried to prevent a vote on a new law governing the country’s central bank.

“These [ruling lawmakers] are criminals and ⁠they deserve tear gas, rubber bullets, cracked skulls and broken bones, not the young people,” Berisha, leader of the Democratic Party of Albania, said.

The protests began in May and were triggered by Rama’s preliminary approval of a luxury resort linked to Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

The student-led protest movement has since evolved into something far bigger, with demonstrators citing economic stagnation, alleged corruption and poor education standards, coupled with high tuition fees.

The anti-government protests are Albania’s largest in decades and have turned violent, injuring hundreds of people, including police officers. Government buildings, banks and private buildings have also been attacked and set on fire.

Rama has been in office for 13 years and has refused to resign after winning a fourth term last year.

As Berisha addressed parliament on Thursday, his colleagues surrounded him while holding photos of protesters allegedly injured by rubber bullets.

Rama has introduced fines of more than $6,000 for anyone who attends a protest that turns violent, even if they did not participate in such acts. That is six times Albania’s average monthly salary of around $1,000.

Rama has announced a series of measures aimed at easing the protests. These include increasing the monthly scholarship stipend for students from low-income families, according to Albania’s public broadcaster, Radio Televizioni Shqiptar. Scholarships have also been extended to master’s degree students. Rama has also announced subsidised rent for students, the broadcaster reported.

news.originalContent:
A Maine resident alleged Thursday that she was tricked into appearing in an advertisement supporting Democratic Maine Senate nominee Troy Jackson.

Laundromat owner Kelly Kusnirak said a videographer interviewed her for what she thought would be part of an advertisement supporting Republican Maine Sen. Susan Collins, according to footage posted by The Maine Wire. The footage later aired in an ad paid for by the Campaign for a Family Friendly Economy (CFFE) in support of Jackson, even though she never agreed to appear in an ad supporting the Maine Democrat.

“I am not a Troy Jackson supporter at all,” Kusnirak said. “I definitely feel like I was misled because when I did finally see the ad, I was like oh wow, look at that banner, Troy Jackson. I was surprised to see that it was Troy Jackson. Totally did not expect that. I thought it was going to be for Susan Collins. If they’re willing to mislead me, how far will they go? And you know, when will it end?”

Kusnirak alleged that a videographer approached her at her laundromat in March or April and identified himself as someone shooting for Collins’ campaign. At the time, Jackson had not replaced former Democratic Maine Senate nominee Graham Platner, who dropped out in July after a woman accused him of rape. (RELATED: Secret Scheme To Sabotage GOP Senator Reveled After Democrat Denied Involvement: REPORT)

A Maine woman claims a videographer told her she would be appearing in an ad for Sen. Susan Collins… She was shocked when the ad came out, and it was for Troy Jackson. "If they’re willing to mislead me, how far will they go." https://t.co/TZSXCPQOSD

The ad showed Kusnirak stating that “nothing is affordable in Maine” and that the state lacks good-paying jobs or wages, according to The Robinson Report. The ad ended with footage of Jackson and words that said, “Susan Collins is too expensive for Maine. VOTE TROY JACKSON FOR SENATE IN NOVEMBER.”

“As far as affordability in Maine, nothing is affordable in Maine,” Kusnirak said in the ad. “Rent is not affordable, buying a house is not affordable, but do our wages go up? Do we have good jobs in Maine? No.”

Kusnirak said she only found out about the ad when a friend saw it. She stated that Collins “always puts Maine first” and has done more for affordability than the state Legislature.

The CFFE PAC paid for the ad, which spent over $1.6 million in support of Jackson, according to The Political Group. CFFE did not respond to the Daily Caller News Foundation’s request for comment.

“I said yes because I support Susan,” Kusnirak continued. “I had no idea that months later my face and my words would show up in an ad for her opponent. I feel like I was duped.”
